'''''Portulacaria afra''''' (known as '''elephant bush''', '''porkbush''', '''purslane tree''', '''dwarf jade''' and '''''{{lang|af|spekboom}}''''' in [[Afrikaans]]) is a small-leaved [[succulent plant]] found in [[South Africa]]. These succulents commonly have a reddish stem and green [[Leaf|leaves]], but a variegated [[cultivar]] is often seen in cultivation. They are simple to care for and make easy houseplants for a sunny location. In frost-free regions they may be used in outdoor landscaping.

==Description==
It is a soft-wooded, semi-evergreen upright shrub or small tree, usually {{convert|2.5|-|4.5|m|ft|0}} tall. ''P. afra'' has smaller and rounder pads and more compact growth (shorter internodal spaces, down to {{convert|1.5|mm}}). It is much hardier, faster growing, more loosely branched, and has more limber tapering branches than ''Crassula'' once established.<ref>
{{cite web
 |title=''Portulacaria afra''
 |type=monograph
 |publisher=Pyramid Dancer
 |website=magiminiland.org
 |url=http://www.magiminiland.org/Portulacaria.html
 |access-date=2011-01-20
}}
</ref>

The genus ''[[Portulacaria]]'' has been shown to be an outlier, relatively unrelated to the other genera in the family, which are all restricted to small ranges in the arid far west of [[Southern Africa]].<ref name="BruynsOliveira-Neto2014" />

==Distribution and habitat==
It is very widespread in the east of [[South Africa]] (as well as [[Eswatini]]). In this moist climate, it is relatively rare, and tends to favour dryer rocky outcrops and slopes.

It is also found in much denser numbers in the dryer southern Cape. Here it occurs from the [[Little Karoo]] of the [[Western Cape]], eastwards up until the [[thicket]] vegetation of the [[Eastern Cape]].<ref name="guralnick"/> Spekboom is found most prolifically in the [[Albany thickets]], a woodland [[ecoregion]], which locally is often called ''{{lang|af|noorsveld}}'', after the high number of succulent ''[[Euphorbia]]'' species, which are often called ''{{lang|af|noors}}'' plants.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://treesa.org/portulacaria-afra/|title=Portulacaria afra {{!}} Tree SA|last=Becking|first=David|language=en-ZA|access-date=2019-07-21}}</ref> In these environments, ''P. afra'' is a source of food for multiple large herbivores, such as the [[black rhinoceros]] and the [[African elephant]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Paley|first1=R. G. T.|last2=Kerley|first2=G. I. H.|date=1998-07-31|title=The winter diet of elephant in Eastern Cape Subtropical Thicket, Addo Elephant National Park|url=https://koedoe.co.za/index.php/koedoe/article/view/244|journal=Koedoe|language=en|volume=41|issue=1|pages=37–45|doi=10.4102/koedoe.v41i1.244|issn=2071-0771|doi-access=free}}</ref> Although it is not the primary food source for these animals, it still makes up a significant portion of their diet.<ref name=":0" />

''P. afra'' is considered a keystone species in the shrubland thicket [[Subregion|subregions]] of the Albany thickets due to its resistance to drought, flood, and fire. When it is not the dominant species, spekboom borders shrubland thickets and protects interior growth. Its growth rate is not dependent on water availability, and spekboom is able to accumulate [[biomass]] in excess of what would be predicted by rainfall levels in the area.<ref name=":3">South African National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI). 2021. [https://www.sanbi.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/2021_Ecosystem-Guidelines-for-the-Albany-Thicket-Biome.pdf Ecosystem Guidelines for the Albany Thicket Biome]. South African National Biodiversity Institute, an entity of the Department of Environment, Forestry and Fisheries, Pretoria. <nowiki>http://hdl.handle.net/20.500.12143/7456</nowiki>.</ref> Despite its ecological significance, [[Ecology|ecologists]] in the region are advised to avoid introducing spekboom in subregions where it is not already present due to its ability to rapidly gain biomass. <ref name=":3" />

==Cultivation and uses==
[[File:Yaiza La Hoya - LZ-2-LZ-703 - Portulacaria afra 02 ies.jpg|thumb|right|"Prostrata" decumbent variety]]
In the wilds of South Africa, large plants do survive the winter frosts by growing dense enough to provide their own natural cover. Drought-tolerant and fire-resistant, it will endure desert sun and heat once established, which the jade plant will not.  ''P. afra'' is a common landscape plant in Phoenix, Arizona, and southern California, growing in [https://planthardiness.ars.usda.gov/ USDA plant hardiness zones] 9–11. [[Cuttings (plant)|Cuttings]] root very easily in most potting media.

===Ornamental===
[[File:Portulacaria afra 2.jpg|thumb|''P. afra'' cultivated as a bonsai]]
It is popular as a specimen for bonsai,<ref name="Ma-Ke_Portulacaria afra ">{{cite web |first=Mark |last=D'Cruz |title=Ma-Ke Bonsai Care Guide for Portulacaria afra |date=6 February 2020 |publisher=Ma-Ke Bonsai |url=https://www.makebonsai.com/post/dwarf-jade |access-date=2021-02-04}}</ref> and as a hardy [[xeriscaping]] plant.

Several varieties exist – some bred in cultivation, others naturally occurring:<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.plantzafrica.com/plantnop/portulacarafra.htm |title=Portulacaria afra |publisher=PlantZAfrica.com |access-date=2015-10-05 |archive-date=2015-09-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924114734/http://www.plantzafrica.com/plantnop/portulacarafra.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref>
* '''"Limpopo"''': A variety with much larger leaves. It is the natural form from the far north of the species' range.
* '''"Prostrata"''': A low-lying, decumbent form that is frequently used as a groundcover.
* '''"Aurea"''': A compact, upright form with rounded leaves that go bright yellow in the sun.
* '''"Foliis variegatus"''': A variegated form.
* '''"Medio-picta"''': Variegated with a lighter centre.

===Culinary===
In Southern Africa it is commonly eaten, usually as one component of a salad or a soup. It should not be confused with the [[jade plant]], which is mildly toxic.{{cn|date=March 2023}}

''P. afra'' is also used to feed livestock during periods of drought due to its [[Succulents|succulent]] nature.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Oakes|first=A.J.|date=December 1973|title=Portulacaria afra Jacq.: A Potential Browse Plant|jstor=4253450|journal=Economic Botany|volume=27|issue=4|pages=413–416|doi=10.1007/BF02860694|bibcode=1973EcBot..27..413O |s2cid=45207710}}</ref> Most commonly used for cattle and goats, these plants also act as a supplemental source of water on top of their nutritional benefits for livestock.<ref name=":1" />

=== Medicinal ===
This is one of the many plants used as a traditional treatment for skin conditions used by people in rural areas that do not have easy access to more modern medicine.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=De Wet|first1=Helene|last2=Nciki|first2=Sibongile|last3=van Vuuren|first3=Sandy F.|date=2013-07-19|title=Medicinal plants used for the treatment of various skin disorders by a rural community in northern Maputaland, South Africa|journal=Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine|volume=9|issue=1|page=51|doi=10.1186/1746-4269-9-51|issn=1746-4269|pmc=3724715|pmid=23870616 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

===Carbon sequestration and ecological impact===
''P. afra'' is capable of either [[C3 carbon fixation|{{c3}}]] or CAM [[carbon fixation]], depending on factors such as the season and the age of the leaves.<ref name="guralnick" /> In the dry season, it relies on the [[Crassulacean acid metabolism|CAM]] pathway due to the lack of water, but when water is reintroduced, the plant quickly reverts to the C<sub>3</sub> pathway in order to conserve energy.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Guralnick|first1=Lonnie J.|last2=Ting|first2=Irwin P.|date=1987-10-01|title=Physiological Changes in Portulacaria afra (L.) Jacq. during a Summer Drought and Rewatering|journal=Plant Physiology|language=en|volume=85|issue=2|pages=481–486|doi=10.1104/pp.85.2.481|issn=0032-0889|pmid=16665724|pmc=1054282|doi-access=free}}</ref> The maturity of the leaf tissue also matters because younger tissue is unable to completely seal the stomata, making CAM impossible.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Guralnick|first1=Lonnie J.|last2=Rorabaugh|first2=Patricia A.|last3=Hanscom|first3=Zac|date=1984-06-01|title=Influence of Photoperiod and Leaf Age on Crassulacean Acid Metabolism in Portulacaria afra (L.) Jacq.|journal=Plant Physiology|language=en|volume=75|issue=2|pages=454–457|doi=10.1104/pp.75.2.454|issn=0032-0889|pmid=16663642|pmc=1066928|doi-access=free}}</ref> So while the older leaves are able to switch pathways based on the season and conditions, the younger leaves have to rely solely on the C<sub>3</sub> pathway. It can sequester a maximum of 15.4'' ''t CO<sub>2</sub> ha<sup>−1</sup>yr<sup>−1</sup>.<ref name="MillsCowling2014" />

The South African government's Working for Ecosystems programme proposes restoring a million hectares (2.5 million acres) of ''P. afra'' thicket.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Matthews |first1=Alexander |title=How shrubs can help solve climate change |url=https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20200203-the-south-african-plant-fighting-climate-change |access-date=4 February 2020 |work=BBC Future |agency=BBC |date=3 February 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=South Africa's Environmental Programmes |url=https://www.environment.gov.za/sites/default/files/docs/publications/nrm_booklet.pdf |access-date=4 February 2020 |archive-date=4 February 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200204220133/https://www.environment.gov.za/sites/default/files/docs/publications/nrm_booklet.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> The addition of more spekboom into the environment can also help restore native species to areas where they no longer can grow.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=Panter|first1=Bryce|last2=Ruwanza|first2=Sheunesu|date=June 2019|title=Spekboom (Portulacaria afra) Planting in Degraded Thickets Improves Soil Properties and Vegetation Diversity.|url=https://web-b-ebscohost-com.lib-proxy.fullerton.edu/ehost/detail/detail?vid=6&sid=399e45f5-20cb-4934-9f55-4973845037e1%40pdc-v-sessmgr06&bdata=JnNpdGU9ZWhvc3QtbGl2ZSZzY29wZT1zaXRl#AN=136790503&db=aph|journal=Ecological Restoration|volume=37|issue=2|pages=76–80|doi=10.3368/er.37.2.76|bibcode=2019EcoRe..37...76P |s2cid=181825218|via=EBSCO|hdl=10019.1/111660|hdl-access=free}}</ref> ''P. afra'' has been shown to help create shade and add organic material into sandy soil, which allows for an environment more hospitable to young plants, thus helping restore populations of native species that were reduced by [[overgrazing]] and [[desertification]].<ref name=":2" />
